title: Seasons in the journal
hookLine: late in life he tracked when each plant flowered, records some scientists still use

lines: A LIST IN THE SPRING CHAPTER.
cards: In Walden's chapter on spring, Thoreau does something a poet usually wouldn't. He lists dates: not of his own life, but the days the ice on Walden Pond broke up, year after year, so he could compare.
In the middle of a rapturous chapter about thawing sand and returning birds sits a little column of records.
The same man who wrote about sucking out the marrow of life also wanted to know exactly when the pond let go of winter.

teach.h: TRAVELED A GOOD DEAL IN CONCORD.
teach.b: First, the habit in Walden. "I have travelled a good deal in Concord," he wrote, half joking: Concord was his home town.
He traveled deep instead of far, and part of that was writing down when things happened: the ice, the first birds, the frogs. Second, the habit grows.
In his later journal the noting turns into lists and tables: when this plant leafed out, when that one flowered, when a bird first sang, season after season in the same fields.
The poet's eye becomes a careful observer's, and he doesn't seem to think of those as enemies. Third, a notebook's long reach. His records have found readers he couldn't have pictured.
Some people who study the seasons have gone back to them to compare flowering times then and now.
A man noting a violet in a field near Concord left something useful to strangers far ahead of him. Fourth, records as practice. Keeping a record sounds dry.
But to know when the maple turns, you have to look at the maple every day.
Records are attention that has been kept, not thrown away. They turn a vague feeling, spring seems early this year, into something you can see.
And they tie you to one patch of ground: you start to belong to a place by knowing its calendar.

how: Some people keep a seasonal record in Thoreau's spirit, noting the dates when one tree leafs out, flowers or turns color, which ties them to one place across the years.

games.q: what does “seasons in the journal” mean?
o: Thoreau's notes on when ice broke and plants flowered
a farmer's almanac predicting next year's weather
poems Thoreau wrote for each of the four seasons

games.q: inside the records: tap the pairs.
p: when the pond's ice broke up

s: Walden contains no dates or records at all
the spring chapter lists when the pond's ice broke up across several years.
Thoreau joked that he had traveled a good deal in Concord
he traveled deep in one town rather than far.
keeping records and looking with wonder can't go together
the same chapter holds both, and his later journal does too.

games.q: you're writing a rapturous chapter about spring. you also know the day the ice broke up in other years. what do you do?
o: leave the numbers out; they spoil the mood.
put the list right in the chapter.
save them for a science paper.
games.why: Thoreau put the ice-out list right into the spring chapter of Walden, wonder and records side by side.

practice: Bring to mind one plant you'll see again, a tree on your street, a weed by the door, a houseplant, or look at it if it's near. Is it in bud, in leaf, in flower, in fruit, or bare, and what color is it at the edges?
Don't decide what it means; just see where it is in its year, as precisely as you can.

wordCard.voice: Seasons in the journal. Thoreau's habit of writing down when the ice broke and the plants flowered, year after year. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: keep records. Attention that's kept becomes the calendar of one place. Same time tomorrow.
